item.title: Lock Your GitHub Actions
item.description:
Source: hugovk.dev

Top Comment:

The advice here is really great (as I'd expect from Hugo), but as the maintainer of zizmor I want to note some caveats with the current iteration of workflow lockfiles:

- They only lock normal action calls. If your workflows invoke other reusable workflows, you need to keep those hash-pinned manually for now.

- Composite actions are not themselves locked. Instead, they get locked transitively through their callsites i.e. the workflows that call them. This makes any individual caller that uses lockfiles safe, but it also makes the current `gh actions-lock` default unsafe (since it removes hash-pins from the composite action itself, meaning that any external caller that invokes the action loses their transitive pinning).

- Other forms of `uses:` clauses, like Docker images, are also not currently locked via the lockfile. And the same for forms of interior mutability (like an action running `npx ...` under the hood, although the latter is fully outside of GitHub's control to prevent. But these mean that you can't assume that a fully locked Actions setup is in fact 100% immutable.

I hope they address these gaps soon, because it's otherwise an excellent (and long-awaited) feature.

item.title: Emacs in the Age of Magic
item.description:
Source: commandlinesystems.com

Top Comment:

There are several points of view here. Some people claim they will never need to "program" again because the LLM will do everything. That text editors are dead... and so is the career of programmer or software engineer. That nowadays, with Claude Code, you can reimplement anything (given a large enough context window, of course). That it is like being an expert in every programming language and system out there. That we should remove politicians and CEOs and put an AI in their place.

On the other hand, many people claim that machine-generated software STINKS. That it is extremely verbose, that it reimplements similar methods over and over again. That it would rather cut corners at a low level than build high-level abstractions. That it pulls in libraries and makes serious security mistakes. That it writes tests that are basically incomplete. That it is unable to synthesize and keep context. In short, it has the same flaws as humans.

I think these are binary points of view, and both are right. We have vampires that are incredibly fast, super-strong, super-intelligent and super-agile, that suck your blood (your money), and that die as soon as the sunlight of security or complexity hits them.

There has to be another way. Nobody questions the versatility LLMs provide, or the boldness they give you to take on new projects. But I am not convinced that programmers or software engineers are going to disappear. I am not convinced that a manager can ship a new feature in a couple of afternoons and then lay off, or skip hiring, a junior or senior developer. There is a line near the beginning of Dune that goes something like this: "there was a time when men handed their thinking over to machines in the hope of being freed, but that only allowed other men with machines to enslave them."

We need to find a new path between smartphone addiction and being dumbed down by LLMs.

item.title: Show HN: Yogurt – Free, private, open-source alternative to Granola
item.description:
Source: github.com

Hey HN, I’m Eric and I want to share an OSS project that I’ve been building in my free time. Yogurt is a free, MIT licensed desktop app that uses on-device AI models to transcribe, summarize, and chat with your meetings.

Here's a quick demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BFfbXAwRq98

Similar to Granola, Yogurt runs in the background and does not join your calls. But unlike Granola, Yogurt is open-source, free to use, and private. Your meeting transcripts, call recordings, and summaries never leave your computer.

As small OSS models have gotten faster and more powerful, Yogurt seemed like a pretty obvious win for privacy and cost conscious folks. You do not need a frontier model to summarize meeting notes or answer questions about them. And if you want to make your notes available to a frontier model, you can just share it with Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. directly via Yogurt’s local MCP server. There’s no need to use a paid cloud service as a middleman.

I tried some of the most popular OSS note taking tools, and most were missing features like calendar integration, MCP server, etc. or required you to connect or create an account. And more than that, they didn’t feel polished enough for it to be something I actually wanted to use daily, and so I built Yogurt to scratch that itch. I spent a lot of time fine-tuning every UI interaction/animation and optimizing the model calls to get the most out of your hardware + make it snappy.

To support Windows/Mac/Linux, I decided to go with Electron. I use whisper.cpp for transcription and Apple’s on-device SpeechAnalyzer if your system supports it. For call summaries and questions, I use a local open weight LLM that automatically gets downloaded and set up based on what your hardware can handle without your cooling fans firing off like crazy (this part uses llama.cpp).

I’ve spent a lot of time working on details like echo detection/reduction, global/folder/local level search respectively, and auto-end recordings. Hope this is useful for any of you who have held out on using AI note tools for privacy or cost reasons, or for folks using cloud tools who want to switch to something free and open source that still feels great to use.

Would love to hear what you think about the onboarding and note taking experience :)

item.title: Atuin Threads: All your agent sessions on every machine
item.description:
Source: blog.atuin.sh

Top Comment:

If you only need this on one machine, I've been using my own tool, "aichat search", for the same thing. It's a Rust TUI over a Tantivy index of your Claude Code and Codex sessions. It indexes the session files in place rather than keeping its own copy.

On my machine, with ~22 GB of sessions, its index is under 1 GB, while Threads added 8.1 GB after importing the same sessions (it stores each conversation twice: once encrypted for sync, once for search). Agents can use it too (aichat search --json), and from a search result you can resume, or carry the work into a new session.

  uv tool install claude-code-tools
  brew install pchalasani/tap/aichat-search   # or: cargo install aichat-search
  aichat search
aichat also has other subcommands for working with sessions: porting one between Claude Code and Codex (or to another provider), rolling over to a fresh session that carries the context, trimming bloated sessions, moving a session to another project or account, etc.

No sync across machines; that's where Threads is nicer. Also Threads seems to show sub-agent relations and live-status, which mine doesn't. I like my TUI interface better though.

item.title: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG
item.description:
Source: machinelearning.apple.com

Top Comment:

Just yesterday I saw a talk from Spotify where they presented their own fast retrieval mechanism "Parallel Fusion Router" [1]. It's also in the "learned retrieval" paradigm - in their case they use a teacher LLM to train a much smaller router LLM how to retrieve, using an LLM-as-a-judge based reward function.

From my own experience, these learned methods from Apple, Spotify and others, are highly relevant to hyperscale only - when you are dealing with hundreds of millions of items to choose from (or more), and require super high relevance in the top-5. For all other use cases (up to a few million items) I found that just building a BM25 index, and giving the LLM a BM25 "search tool" and casting a "wide net" wins every single time compared to learned methods (though the latter are more publishable in recsys and icml).

[1] https://research.atspotify.com/2025/9/you-say-search-i-say-r...
